chunks: Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Faddal from Amr ibn Sa'id from Musaddiq ibn Sadah from Ammar ibn Musa al-Sabati from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who has missed days from the month of Ramadan, how should he make them up? He said: 'If he has two days to make up, he should fast one day and break the fast (skip one day) between them; and if he has five days, he should break the fast on some days between them, and he is not permitted to fast more than six consecutive days; and if he has eight or ten days, he should break the fast on one day between them.'

The meaning in this narration is that whoever is obligated to make up the month of Ramadan is not required to make them up consecutively, according to what was obligatory for him initially. What this report contains regarding the command to break the fast and separate between these days is merely a recommendation (choice) rather than an obligation, and we have previously established that making them up consecutively is superior.

key_terms.قَضَاءُ شَهْرِ رَمَضَانَ: Making up missed fasts of Ramadan
key_terms.يُفْطِرْ بَيْنَهُمَا: To break the fast between them (skip a day)

ai.seo_question: How should a Muslim make up missed Ramadan fasts according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), the ruling for making up missed Ramadan fasts is clarified as a matter of choice rather than strict obligation, with specific instructions to intersperse fasting days based on the quantity of missed days. The accompanying commentary by Shaykh al-Tusi emphasizes that while consecutive makeup is superior (afdal), the command to fast for no more than six consecutive days serves as a recommendation to prevent hardship, reflecting the Shia principle of ease in religious obligations.
